title: A Million People, One Game Boy
hook: An anonymous programmer let the chat control the game. More than a million people played the same Pokémon at once.
situation: Live streams were something you watched. The chat beside them was a place to talk, not to take part in what happened on screen.
exchange: In February 2014 an anonymous Australian programmer streamed Pokémon Red on Twitch with a script that turned every chat message such as up or A into a button press, so the whole audience played together.
brought: The programmer
A simple, open idea and a stream that ran around the clock.
The audience
Over a million players, plus the jokes, art and legends that grew around their chaos.
turning_point: After 16 days, on 1 March 2014, the crowd finished the game. About 1.16 million people had entered a command and the stream drew around 36 million views, a Guinness World Record for the most people playing a single-player game.
metric_label: People who sent a command, a Guinness World Record
measure: Participants counted by the stream’s own script and recognised by Guinness World Records
evidence: The participant count, views and duration are well recorded, including on Twitch’s own blog. It shows participation, the strongest form of attention, but nobody earned money from it directly.
lesson: The audience will play if you give them controls. Interactive formats turn viewers into a community faster than anything else.
take: Twitch Plays Pokémon is the purest community case in the archive. Nobody was the star, and that was the point. Every interactive stream and game show on Twitch since owes something to it.

creative.label: Read Twitch’s post on the victory
creative.heading: Creator media

announcement: Read Twitch’s post on the victory
links: See the record entry · Guinness World Records
how_to_measure: For an interactive format, measure the share of viewers who take an action, and how long they stay compared with ordinary streams.

title: Dooced
hook: She was sacked for writing about work on her blog. Her name became the word for it, and the blog became her job.
situation: In 2002 blogs were personal sites read by friends and a few strangers. Writing honestly about your life online had no rules, and no one had made it a career.
exchange: Heather Armstrong wrote dooce.com, a funny, candid blog that included stories about her workplace. When her employer found it, she was fired.
brought: Heather Armstrong
Sharp, honest writing about work, depression and later motherhood.
Her readers
An audience that grew into millions and made the blog a business.
turning_point: To be dooced came to mean being fired for something you wrote online. Armstrong turned the blog into one of the first personal sites to support a family through advertising, and became a founding figure of parenting blogs.
metric_label: The year she was fired for her blog
measure: A date. Advertising income from the blog was discussed in interviews but not fully published
evidence: The firing, the word and the blog’s later success are well documented in contemporary and later reporting. Revenue figures were reported in interviews rather than disclosed.
lesson: Candour builds an audience, and it has consequences. Agree clear rules about what creators can share, and protect people who share honestly.
take: Dooce is where personal life became publishing. Every vlogger, every family channel and every workplace social media policy descends from this moment.

creative.label: Read a history of being fired for a blog · Daily Dot
creative.heading: Creator media

announcement: Read how blogging got risky · NBC News
impact_source: Read about the Dooce effect · Business Standard
how_to_measure: For personal publishing, track returning readers and the share who subscribe or follow across channels, the signal that an audience trusts the writer rather than one post.

title: The Whisper Genre
hook: She whispered and folded towels on camera. Millions of people used her videos to fall asleep.
situation: Some people felt a calming tingle from soft sounds and close attention, but had no name for it and no content made for it. Online video was built on loud, fast entertainment.
exchange: Maria Viktorovna began uploading videos as Gentle Whispering in 2011, whispering, tapping and role-playing quiet, caring scenes designed to trigger what people now call ASMR.
brought: Maria Viktorovna
Patient, carefully recorded videos and a gentle on-screen manner.
The ASMR community
Viewers who shared the name, the triggers and their own videos.
turning_point: Her channel became one of the first ASMR channels with a mass audience, and the genre spread into thousands of channels, sleep apps and advertising that borrowed its sounds.
measure: A date. The genre’s size is clear from the number of channels, not from one measured figure
evidence: Rolling Stone’s oral history and CNBC’s reporting document how the genre formed and her role in it. The evidence shows a format taking hold rather than a commercial result.
lesson: Some formats serve a need, not a moment. Look for content people use as a tool, for sleep, study or calm, because they come back every day.
take: ASMR shows the creator economy finding audiences no broadcaster would have commissioned for. A quiet woman with a good microphone built a genre.

creative.label: Watch the first whisper video · Gentle Whispering
creative.heading: Creator media

impact_source: Read An Oral History of ASMR · Rolling Stone
how_to_measure: For utility formats, measure repeat viewing per person and time of day. A video watched every night is a different asset from one watched once.

title: Six Seconds
hook: A comedian wrote sketches that lasted six seconds. He became the most followed person on Vine.
situation: Vine, launched in 2013, limited every video to six looping seconds. Most users posted clips of their day. Few thought you could tell a joke with a set-up and a punchline in that time.
exchange: Andrew Bachelor, known as King Bach, wrote and acted tightly edited sketches with friends, often featuring other Vine stars, landing a twist in the final second.
brought: King Bach
Comic timing built for the loop and a stream of collaborations.
Vine
A format with one rule, and a feed that rewarded whatever made people watch twice.
turning_point: In March 2015 he passed Nash Grier to become the most followed account on Vine. Short-form comedy became a training ground for a generation of creators who moved to TikTok, YouTube and television.
metric_label: Most followed account on Vine, March 2015
measure: A follower ranking, reported by Tubefilter
evidence: The ranking is documented. It shows his reach on Vine, and his later film and television roles show the crossover. Vine’s shutdown, in Edition 05, shows the risk of depending on one platform.
lesson: Constraints create formats. A strict limit forces creators to find a structure that the audience learns to love.
take: King Bach proved that six seconds was enough for a joke. TikTok inherited Vine’s best creators and its best idea: short, loopable, rewatchable.

how_to_measure: For short loops, measure replays per viewer and completion rate. A loop watched three times is worth more than three views from different people.

title: The Podcast Everyone Talked About
hook: A radio journalist re-examined one murder case over twelve episodes. Podcasting suddenly had a hit.
situation: Podcasts had existed for a decade but were a niche, mostly radio shows repackaged for download. Few had mass audiences, and advertisers barely noticed them.
exchange: Sarah Koenig and the team behind This American Life released Serial, a weekly investigation into a 1999 murder in Baltimore, told one episode at a time with the reporting still in progress.
brought: Sarah Koenig and Julie Snyder
Investigative reporting, a cliffhanger structure and a voice listeners trusted.
Listeners
Weekly downloads, theories and conversations that spread the show by word of mouth.
turning_point: In November 2014 Serial became the fastest podcast to reach five million downloads and streams on iTunes. Podcasts became a mainstream format and a market advertisers chased.
metric_label: Downloads and streams, the fastest to get there on iTunes
measure: Downloads and streams reported by Apple, a count of attention, not of revenue
evidence: Apple’s figures were widely reported. They show the scale of listening; the show’s sponsorship income and the wider growth of the industry are documented separately.
lesson: Serialised storytelling builds a habit. Give the audience a reason to come back next week, and they will bring others.
take: Serial is the moment audio became a creator medium worth taking seriously. Every podcast deal in Edition 03 rests on the audience habit it created.

creative.label: Read about the record · The Irish Times
creative.heading: Creator media

announcement: Read why millions were listening · Atlanta Journal-Constitution
impact_source: Read about the record · The Irish Times
how_to_measure: For a serialised show, track the share of listeners to episode one who reach the final episode, and how quickly new listeners start from the beginning.

title: Lost at Sea
hook: A producer got lost on a jet ski at night and filmed it. Snapchat stories became a stage.
situation: Snapchat’s disappearing stories were used for private moments between friends. Celebrities used polished posts on other platforms and barely touched it.
exchange: DJ Khaled posted daily stories full of motivational slogans, which he called keys, and narrated his life as it happened. In December 2015 he filmed himself lost on a jet ski off Miami at night.
brought: DJ Khaled
Unfiltered energy, catchphrases and a willingness to post everything.
Snapchat
A format that rewarded the raw, the immediate and the slightly absurd.
turning_point: The jet ski story spread far beyond Snapchat and made Khaled one of the most watched people on the app. His slogans became a book and his profile rose with it, showing celebrities what stories could do.
metric_label: When the jet ski story went viral
measure: A date. Snapchat did not publish story view counts
evidence: The episode and its impact on his career are well reported by Billboard, NPR and others. Snapchat did not publish view figures, so the reach is shown by coverage rather than counts.
lesson: Narrate as it happens. A format built on immediacy rewards people who show the unedited version of their day.
take: Khaled turned Snapchat stories into a show before Instagram copied the format. The jet ski is silly, and it taught a generation of celebrities to behave like creators.

title: Chewbacca Mom
hook: A mother laughed in a Chewbacca mask in a car park. It became the most watched Facebook Live video ever.
situation: Facebook launched Live in 2016 and paid publishers and celebrities to use it. The company wanted a breakthrough moment for the format.
exchange: Candace Payne went live from her car to show her children a Chewbacca mask she had bought, and laughed so hard at herself that she could barely speak.
brought: Candace Payne
Unscripted joy that anyone could share.
Facebook
A new live feature and a feed that pushed it to friends and their friends.
turning_point: The video passed 136 million views within days, the most for a Facebook Live, and Payne was invited to Facebook’s headquarters and onto television. Facebook named it the top live video of 2016.
metric_label: Views within days, a Facebook Live record
measure: Views as reported by Facebook, which counted a view after three seconds
evidence: The view count is from Facebook and recorded by Guinness World Records. Facebook’s view definition was generous, which matters when comparing it with other platforms.
lesson: Platforms launch features with paid talent, but the moment that sells the format is usually an ordinary person. Watch for them and amplify them.
take: Facebook paid media companies millions for live video, and a mother in a car park beat them all for free. It is the clearest example of a platform being taught its own product by a user.

title: Beats to Relax and Study To
hook: An animated girl studies by a window while music plays, forever. It was a live stream that never stopped, until a false claim took it down.
situation: Live streams were events with a start and an end. Music on YouTube meant individual videos and playlists.
exchange: A French music curator known as Dimitri ran a channel, first called ChilledCow, that streamed relaxed lo-fi hip hop around the clock over a looping animation of a girl studying, later named Lofi Girl.
brought: Lofi Girl’s creators
A calm loop, careful curation and a label for independent producers.
Listeners
Millions who kept the stream on while they studied or worked, and a chat that never slept.
turning_point: The format was copied across YouTube and became a genre of its own. In July 2022 a stream that had run for about two years was taken down by a false copyright claim, prompting a public outcry until YouTube restored it.
metric_label: Continuous run of the stream before the false takedown, 2022
measure: The length of one stream, as reported by TechCrunch and NPR
evidence: The format’s influence and the takedown are well documented. The channel’s revenue, including from its record label, is not public.
lesson: A stream can be a place rather than a show. And any creator who depends on one platform depends on its systems for handling false claims.
take: Lofi Girl turned YouTube into a radio station people keep on all day. The takedown shows how fragile even the most loved creator assets are when automated systems get it wrong.
impact_source: Read about the debate it reignited · NPR
how_to_measure: For an always-on stream, measure concurrent listeners by hour and how many return daily. It behaves like radio and should be measured like it.

image.alt: An illustrated girl wears headphones and writes at a desk beside her cat
image.credit: Official current radio artwork, substituted still; original 2017 stream not authenticated · Lofi Girl

title: The App That Became TikTok
hook: A lip-sync app popular with American teenagers was bought and switched off. Its users woke up on TikTok.
situation: Musical.ly, founded in Shanghai by Alex Zhu and Luyu Yang, had built a huge young audience in the United States making lip-sync and dance videos. ByteDance had a similar app, Douyin, at home and TikTok abroad.
exchange: ByteDance bought Musical.ly in late 2017, in a deal reported at about $1 billion. In August 2018 it merged the apps, moving every Musical.ly account to TikTok.
brought: Musical.ly’s creators
Millions of young American users and the lip-sync and dance formats they had built.
ByteDance
TikTok’s recommendation feed, which showed videos from strangers rather than friends.
turning_point: The merger gave TikTok a ready-made Western audience and their formats. Combined with its recommendation feed, it grew into the platform that reshaped short video worldwide.
metric_label: When Musical.ly was merged into TikTok
measure: A date. User numbers at the merger were reported by the companies and varied
evidence: The merger is documented by TechCrunch and The Next Web, and the purchase price was reported. TikTok’s later growth is well documented, but how much came from Musical.ly’s users is not separated.
lesson: Formats travel with their creators. When a platform buys an audience, it is buying the habits the creators taught them.
take: Musical.ly invented the lip-sync dance culture TikTok became famous for. Its creators moved over and kept going, and most never noticed the change of owner.
impact_source: Read about the change · The Next Web
how_to_measure: After merging platforms, track how many active creators keep posting after 30 and 90 days, and how quickly the new feed finds them an audience.

image.alt: The TikTok musical-note mark and white TikTok lettering on black
image.credit: Later official TikTok mark, cropped from 2020 announcement artwork; no original 2018 merger video authenticated · TikTok / ByteDance

title: A Game Made by Players
hook: Two players built a pet game inside Roblox. At its peak it had more people playing at once than the biggest games on Steam.
situation: Hit games were made by studios with large budgets. Roblox let anyone build games on its platform and earn from them, but few expected a player-made game to rival commercial releases.
exchange: Adopt Me!, created by Roblox developers NewFissy and Bethink, let players adopt, raise and trade pets. Regular updates, like new eggs and pets, brought players back in waves.
brought: The developers
Simple, social gameplay and steady updates that gave players a reason to return.
Roblox
Free distribution to millions of young players and a way to earn from in-game purchases.
turning_point: In October 2019 an update pushed Adopt Me! past 1.6 million concurrent players, a record for Roblox. Its team went on to form Uplift Games, a studio built on a player-made hit.
metric_label: Concurrent players, a Roblox record in 2019
measure: Peak concurrent players, reported by GameSpot and the developers
evidence: The concurrency record is documented. In-game revenue was not published in detail, so the commercial result is visible only through the studio’s growth.
lesson: On platforms that let anyone build, creators can become studios. Brands entering games should partner with the people already making what players love.
take: Adopt Me! is the creator economy inside a game. It shows that the next generation of creators may be building worlds rather than filming videos.
impact_source: Read about the developers founding Uplift Games · PC Games Insider
how_to_measure: For a game built on a platform, track daily active players, update-day peaks and spend per player over time.

image.alt: Adopt Me illustrated pets above Adopt Collect Trade lettering
image.credit: Current official game key art, substituted still; original record-setting update footage not authenticated · Uplift Games

title: Club Quarantine
hook: A DJ played records from his flat in the first week of lockdown. Michelle Obama, Oprah and 100,000 others showed up.
situation: In March 2020 clubs and venues closed overnight and people were cut off from each other. Instagram Live was used for short chats, not events.
exchange: Derrick Jones, known as D-Nice, went live on Instagram and played music for hours from his home, shouting out viewers by name as they joined.
brought: D-Nice
A DJ’s instinct for a crowd, a deep record collection and warmth on the mic.
The audience
People desperate for company, sharing the stream with friends until famous names arrived.
turning_point: On 21 March 2020 his stream drew more than 100,000 people at once, including Michelle Obama, Oprah Winfrey and Joe Biden. Club Quarantine became a recurring event and a template for virtual concerts.
measure: Concurrent viewers, as reported. Instagram’s live viewer cap meant some couldn’t get in
evidence: The numbers and the famous guests were widely reported by NPR, BET and others. The stream had no ticket or revenue, so its value showed in what came next: partnerships and a voter registration event with Michelle Obama.
lesson: In a moment of shared need, warmth beats production. Respond to what people are feeling, quickly, with what you already have.
take: Club Quarantine made a social feature into a venue. It also showed that a creator’s role can be to host, making the audience feel seen as they arrive.

creative.medium: Later 2021 interview about Club Quarantine; original March 2020 Instagram stream not authenticated
creative.label: Watch the later Club Quarantine interview · ESPN
creative.heading: Creator media

how_to_measure: For a live event on social, track peak concurrency, average minutes watched and how many viewers return to the next one.

image.credit: Later 2021 interview about Club Quarantine; original March 2020 Instagram stream not authenticated · ESPN

title: The Day TikTok Went Dark in India
hook: India banned TikTok overnight. Its creators lost their audiences, and every rival raced to take them in.
situation: India was TikTok’s largest market by users, with creators in small towns building audiences in dozens of languages, many earning for the first time.
exchange: On 29 June 2020, after border clashes with China, India’s government banned TikTok and 58 other Chinese apps. Creators had to rebuild elsewhere.
brought: India’s creators
Audiences in many languages, and the skill to rebuild quickly.
Rival platforms
Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts and Indian apps, all launched or pushed in India within months.
turning_point: Instagram launched Reels in India in July 2020 and YouTube tested Shorts there first in September. Many creators rebuilt their audiences on the new formats, and India became the proving ground for TikTok’s rivals.
metric_label: Indian TikTok users who lost access, as reported
measure: Reported user numbers before the ban, not audited
evidence: The ban, the launch of Reels and Shorts in India and creators’ experiences are well documented by NPR, Forbes and others. Exactly how many creators moved, and what they earn now, is not measured.
lesson: Creators should own a way to reach their audience that no single platform controls. Brands should build programmes that can move with creators.
take: This case is the creator economy’s biggest stress test. It shows how quickly audiences move when a platform disappears, and how fast rivals arrive to welcome them.

title: Minecraft Manhunt
hook: A faceless creator played Minecraft while friends tried to hunt him down. In 2020 Minecraft was the most watched game on YouTube.
situation: Minecraft was more than ten years old and seen as a children’s game past its peak. The big gaming names had moved on to newer titles.
exchange: Dream, who never showed his face, made Manhunt videos in which he raced to finish the game while friends tried to stop him. He and his friends also ran a role-play server whose story played out across many channels.
brought: Dream
High-stakes challenges, sharp editing and a mystery about who he was.
His friends and fans
Collaborations, fan art and clips that carried the story across platforms.
turning_point: In 2020 YouTube said Minecraft videos drew 201 billion views, making it the most watched game on the platform, and Dream was one of the fastest-growing creators of the year.
metric_label: Minecraft video views on YouTube in 2020
measure: Views for the whole game across every creator, reported by YouTube. Not Dream’s views alone
evidence: YouTube’s 2020 gaming figures confirm Minecraft’s revival. Dream’s growth in that year is documented, but the figure covers every Minecraft creator.
lesson: An old game can find new life through new creators. Watch what creators are doing with your product, not only what your marketing team planned.
take: Dream brought the story back to games. His friends’ server became a shared drama played across dozens of channels, which is a model for collaborative creator storytelling.

creative.label: Watch the original 2020 Manhunt episode · Dream
creative.heading: Creator media

announcement: Read about YouTube Gaming’s biggest year · RouteNote
impact_source: Read about Minecraft’s year on YouTube · TheGamer
how_to_measure: For games, track views of creator content against active players by month. When creator views lead, players follow.

title: A Million Dollars a Day
hook: Snapchat launched a TikTok rival and paid a million dollars a day to the people who posted the best videos.
situation: TikTok had taken the short-video audience and Snapchat needed creators fast. Its own app had been built for friends, not for public creators.
exchange: In November 2020 Snap launched Spotlight, a feed of public short videos, and said it would share more than $1 million a day among the creators of the top videos.
brought: Spotlight creators
Short videos made for a new feed, from known names and unknowns alike.
Snap
Cash to get the feed started, and a recommendation system to fill it.
turning_point: Some creators earned hundreds of thousands of dollars in weeks. Snap later said creators had earned more than $250 million on Snapchat in 2021, before the daily prize model was replaced.
metric_label: Paid to Spotlight creators at launch
measure: Snap’s stated payout. Individual earnings were reported by creators
evidence: Snap announced the payouts and later the 2021 total. The fund helped Spotlight start, but Snap reduced it over time and the long-term effect on creators is not published.
deal_value: More than $1 million a day at launch
lesson: Cash can start a format, but it can’t sustain one. Creators stay where their audience is, and money that runs out leaves with them.
take: Spotlight shows how hard it is to buy a creator ecosystem. Paying for the best videos brought creators in. Keeping them needed an audience Snap was still building.
links: Read about creators’ 2021 earnings · Free Malaysia Today
how_to_measure: For a launch fund, track how many paid creators keep posting after payments fall, and the share of the feed’s views their videos still earn.

image.alt: The black outlined Snapchat ghost on a yellow background
image.credit: Official Snap newsroom mark, substituted still; original Spotlight launch video not authenticated · Snap Inc.

title: The Room Everyone Wanted to Be In
hook: An invite-only app for live conversation was the hottest thing in tech. Within months the rooms emptied.
situation: With people stuck at home in 2020 and 2021, live audio offered conversation without cameras. Clubhouse, invitation only, made it feel exclusive.
exchange: Hosts ran live rooms on tech, money, music and culture, and celebrities dropped in. Clubhouse launched a creator programme to support its most popular hosts.
brought: The hosts
Daily shows built on conversation, with no edit and no camera.
Clubhouse
Scarcity, celebrity appearances and a brief monopoly on social audio.
turning_point: Downloads peaked at about 9.6 million in February 2021, then fell to about 900,000 by April as lockdowns eased and Twitter, Spotify and others copied the format.
measure: App downloads estimated by Sensor Tower, as reported by Business Insider. Downloads, not active users
evidence: Download estimates from Sensor Tower show the rise and the fall. The company did not publish reliable active user figures, and how hosts earned is not documented in detail.
lesson: A format that depends on a moment needs a reason to stay when the moment passes. Exclusivity brings people in. Habit keeps them.
take: Clubhouse is the platform-first case that went wrong in public. Its hosts were creators without a way to keep what they made, because nothing was recorded and nothing could be watched later.
